patients.summary: Administrative assistant who joined in 2022 with chronic low back pain treated for decades with daily OTC ibuprofen. In April 2025 she was admitted with alveolar hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis from GPA, leaving stage 3b CKD on prednisone and rituximab; in August 2026 outside nephrology diagnosed nephrogenic diabetes insipidus after her last practice visit.

documents.title: New Patient Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
44F here to establish care and for a physical. Prior PCP was across the river; records requested today.

Concerns: none acute. Low back has bothered her on and off since her early 20s, worse after long days at the desk. Never had imaging or PT for it. Manages with store-brand ibuprofen, usually two 200 mg tabs most days, sometimes skips a day. No leg pain, numbness, weakness, bladder or bowel change.

PMH: chronic mechanical low back pain.
PSH: endoscopic sinus surgery 2020 (outside ENT; she says chronic sinus trouble, much better since).
Meds: OTC ibuprofen as above. No prescriptions. No supplements.
Allergies: none to drugs.
Family: mother with rheumatoid arthritis. Father has high blood pressure and kidney disease. A maternal aunt has type 1 diabetes.
Social: administrative assistant, full time. Never smoked. Wine socially, a glass or two a week. No drug use.
Screening: last Pap she thinks 2019. Mammogram last year, normal per patient. No colonoscopy yet.

Exam: comfortable, well appearing. HEENT clear, nasal mucosa unremarkable. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement or nodes. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear throughout. Abdomen soft, nontender. Back: mild paraspinal tightness low lumbar, no midline tenderness, SLR negative both sides. Strength, reflexes and sensation normal in the legs. Skin without rash. Speculum exam normal; Pap/HPV collected. Breast exam deferred to imaging per her preference.

PHQ-2: 0.

A/P
1. Health maintenance. CMP, CBC, lipids. One-time HCV and HIV screens, she agreed. Pap/HPV sent. Screening mammogram ordered. Colon screening due at 45; will raise next year.
2. Chronic low back pain, mechanical. Reviewed posture, core work, desk setup. She is using ibuprofen most days; talked about taking the least that works and not stacking with other NSAIDs. She would rather not try PT right now.

Return in a year for her physical, sooner as needed.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Dawn, your blood work from Wednesday is back and looks good: kidney and liver tests, blood counts and cholesterol are all in a healthy range. The hepatitis C and HIV screens were negative. The Pap result takes a couple of weeks and I will send a note when it comes in. Please go ahead and book the mammogram if you haven't yet.

documents.title: Records from prior primary care office
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: 38 pages arrived by secure fax from her prior primary care office, covering 2017 through early 2022. Indexed to the chart. Summary for the PCP: yearly physicals with normal labs; Tdap given 09/2019; ENT referral in 2019 for recurrent sinus symptoms, endoscopic sinus surgery done 2020 at an outside surgical center; screening mammogram 2021 read as negative; no medication list beyond OTC ibuprofen for back pain; no allergies on file.

documents.title: Pap result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your Pap and HPV test came back normal. With both negative, the next one is due in five years (2027).

reports.text: Bilateral screening digital mammography with tomosynthesis. Comparison: 2021 outside study. The breasts are heterogeneously dense, which may obscure small masses. No suspicious mass, architectural distortion or suspicious calcifications in either breast. Skin and nipples unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: BI-RADS 1, negative. Routine annual screening recommended.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Back worse x10 days, no particular trigger she can name. Achy band across the low back, stiff in the morning, better once moving. No radiation below the knee, no numbness or weakness, no fever, no urinary or bowel trouble, no weight loss.
Taking ibuprofen 400 mg most days, up to three times on the worst days. Heat helps.

Exam: moves carefully but gets on the table without help. Bilateral lumbar paraspinal spasm and tenderness, no spinous tenderness. Flexion limited by pain. SLR negative. Heel and toe walk fine. Knee and ankle reflexes 2+ and symmetric. Sensation intact.

A/P: acute on chronic mechanical low back pain, no red flags, no imaging needed.
- PT referral, she is willing this time.
- Heat, walking, avoid bed rest.
- Ibuprofen: ok short-term at the lowest dose that works, with food, and back down to occasional use once this settles. Acetaminophen is an alternative.
- Return if not improving in 4-6 weeks or new leg symptoms.

documents.title: Physical therapy initial evaluation
documents.author: physical therapy
documents.body:
Outpatient physical therapy initial evaluation. Referral: chronic low back pain with recent flare.
Subjective: low back ache for many years, flared in late January without a clear trigger. Sits at a desk most of the day. Pain today 4/10.
Objective: lumbar flexion about 75% of expected, extension full with end-range discomfort. Hip flexor and hamstring tightness bilaterally. Core endurance reduced. Neuro screen of the lower limbs normal. No directional preference.
Assessment: mechanical low back pain with deconditioning and postural contributors. Good rehab potential.
Plan: twice weekly for 6 weeks; mobility, core stabilization, hip strengthening, home program, workstation advice.
Thank you for the referral.

documents.title: Back update
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Just wanted to say PT has really helped, the back is mostly back to its usual. Doing the exercises at lunch. I have two more sessions. Thanks!

documents.title: RE: Back update
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Great to hear. Keep up the home program after PT wraps up, that is what keeps it from coming back.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Yearly visit. Feeling well. Back has been decent since PT in the spring; does the stretches a few times a week. Still takes ibuprofen 200-400 mg on bad days, she estimates most days of the week. No new symptoms, no sinus trouble since surgery.

Meds: OTC ibuprofen. NKDA.
Social unchanged: same job, never smoker, wine a couple times a week at most.

Exam: well. Nose and throat normal. No lymphadenopathy. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen benign. Back nontender today, full flexion. No edema. Skin normal.

PHQ-2 0.

Plan:
- Annual labs: CMP, CBC, lipids.
- Colon screening: 45 now; prefers colonoscopy over stool test. GI referral placed.
- Mammogram due next month, ordered.
- Pap up to date (2022, co-test negative).
- Back: continue home exercises.
See her in a year.

documents.title: Colonoscopy report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outside endoscopy center. Indication: average-risk colorectal cancer screening, age 46, no prior colonoscopy.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care. Bowel preparation good throughout.
Findings: the cecum was reached and confirmed by the appendiceal orifice and ileocecal valve. Withdrawal time 9 minutes. Mucosa normal in the entire colon and rectum. No polyps or masses.
Impression: normal screening colonoscopy.
Recommendation: repeat colonoscopy in 10 years. Resume prior diet and activity.

NKDA. Meds: ibuprofen OTC.
Never smoker; occasional wine.

Vitals reviewed. Exam: NAD. TMs and pharynx normal. Neck without nodes or thyromegaly. Heart regular rate, no murmur, rub or gallop. Lungs clear bilaterally. Abdomen soft, no masses. Lumbar ROM full. No edema. Mood and affect normal.
PHQ-2: 1.

Health maintenance: colonoscopy 08/2023 normal, next 2033. Pap/HPV 2022 negative, next 2027. Mammogram due, ordered. Tdap 2019.

Plan: CMP, CBC, lipids today. Flu and COVID in the fall. RTC 1 year.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Dawn, your labs from yesterday are fine overall: blood counts normal, cholesterol in a good place, liver tests normal. Nothing to change. Enjoy the summer.

reports.conclusion: BI-RADS 1, negative. Return to annual screening.

documents.author: RN
documents.body: Here for seasonal vaccines. No fever today, no egg or vaccine reactions in the past. 2024-25 flu IM L arm; 2024-25 Moderna COVID IM R arm. Post-vaccine instructions given; stayed 15 min, no issues.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

documents.title: Same-Day Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Texted this morning about blood when she coughs; seen same day.

Two days of coughing up bright red blood, streaks at first and today about a teaspoon several times. Over the same two days her urine has turned a dark red-brown, like cola. Has felt run down. No chest injury, no recent travel, no new medications other than her usual ibuprofen. Never smoker.

Exam: tired appearing, speaking full sentences. Blood-tinged sputum in a tissue. Nose without active bleeding. Breathing unlabored, lungs without wheeze. Heart regular. No edema. No rash.
Urine dip in office: large blood.

A/P: hemoptysis with what looks like glomerular hematuria. This needs same-day hospital evaluation for a pulmonary-renal process; not safe to work up as an outpatient. Discussed with her and called the regional hospital ED to give report. She has a ride and is leaving now. Will follow from here.

conditions.label: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis with renal involvement

documents.title: Hospital admission notice
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Automated admission notice from the regional hospital: Dawn McGrath admitted 04/28/2025 via the emergency department to the medicine service. Routed to PCP.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital, medicine service. Admitted 04/28/2025, discharged 05/09/2025.

Reason for admission: hemoptysis and hematuria, sent in by her primary care physician.

Course: the hemoptysis was due to diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Kidney function was declining over days with active urine sediment; ANCA testing returned positive for PR3. Nephrology consulted. Percutaneous kidney biopsy showed pauci-immune crescentic necrotizing glomerulonephritis. Diagnosis: granulomatosis with polyangiitis with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Treated with pulse IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisone, and rituximab 1000 mg IV on 05/02, second dose scheduled at the outpatient infusion center 05/16. The bleeding stopped during the first week. Kidney function improved from its worst but did not return to baseline. Ibuprofen stopped permanently given the kidney injury. Calcium and vitamin D started for bone protection on steroids.

Discharge medications: prednisone 40 mg daily, taper per nephrology; calcium carbonate 600 mg three times daily with meals; cholecalciferol 2000 units daily; acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for back pain, no more than 3 g per day. Rituximab second dose 05/16.
Stopped: ibuprofen. Avoid all NSAIDs.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: nephrology within 2-3 weeks; primary care within 1 week.

medications.sig: Take 2 tablets (40 mg) by mouth daily; taper per nephrology
1000 mg IV per nephrology infusion schedule
Take 1 tablet by mouth three times daily with meals
Take 1 tablet by mouth as needed for back pain; no more than 3 g per day

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen 4 days after discharge. Called her on 5/12 when the summary came in.

She was in for 11 days with alveolar hemorrhage and a rapidly progressive GN, and came out with a diagnosis of GPA (PR3-ANCA; crescentic pauci-immune GN on biopsy). Pulse steroids and the first rituximab dose inpatient; second dose is this Friday 5/16 at the infusion center. Nephrology is running the immunosuppression and the taper; first visit with them is scheduled.

Today: no coughing up blood since the first week in the hospital. No shortness of breath walking around the house. Very tired, naps in the afternoon. Urine looks normal color now. Appetite fine. Out of work for now.

Meds reconciled against the discharge list: prednisone 40 mg daily, calcium carbonate 600 mg TID with meals, vitamin D3 2000 units, acetaminophen 500 mg prn (max 3 g/day), rituximab per nephrology. Ibuprofen is off for good; she knows to avoid naproxen and the other OTC NSAIDs as well, and that acetaminophen is the back pain option now.

Exam: tired but comfortable. Lungs clear, no crackles. Heart regular. No edema. Biopsy site on the back healed, no hematoma.

A/P
1. GPA with renal involvement: per nephrology. Labs today, BMP and CBC with diff, copy to nephrology.
2. Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage: resolved clinically.
3. RPGN: kidney function improving; trend per nephrology.
4. Back pain: acetaminophen only.
5. Steroid side effects reviewed (sleep, mood, sugar, appetite).
Call with any blood in sputum, fever or dark urine. Recheck after her nephrology visit.

documents.title: Yesterday's labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your kidney number (creatinine) is 1.78, better than in the hospital but not back to where it used to be; nephrology will be watching that closely. Your blood count is a little low at 11.4, which is expected after the bleeding and the illness. I sent both to the kidney team. Good luck Friday with the infusion.

documents.title: Nephrology follow-up letter
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
Outside nephrology group. Visit 07/31/2025.

Dear colleague,
I saw Ms. McGrath in follow-up for PR3-ANCA vasculitis (GPA) about three months after her admission with pulmonary hemorrhage and crescentic glomerulonephritis.

Since she left the hospital she has felt worn out most days and is down about 5 lb. She describes a vague ache in both knees and wrists without swelling, some constipation, and two episodes of crampy belly pain over the past week. She denies fever, sweats or any infection.
Vitals normal. Her mouth is somewhat dry and she looks a little pale. Lungs clear.
Kidney function is holding steady at the level it reached after the admission. Stool for occult blood is negative. Phosphorus 5.0 mg/dL.

Impression: GPA in remission on induction. The acute glomerulonephritis has settled into chronic kidney disease, stage 3b, from the vasculitic injury on a background of many years of daily NSAID use.

Plan:
- Prednisone is now 10 mg daily and will stay there for now.
- Rituximab maintenance 1000 mg IV every 6 months; next in November.
- Low-phosphate diet handout given. Calcium acetate 667 mg three times daily with meals; stop the calcium carbonate.
- Continue vitamin D3 2000 units. Vitamin D metabolites (25-hydroxy and 1,25-dihydroxy) sent.
- No NSAIDs.
Return in about 6 months.

Medications: prednisone 10 mg daily, rituximab as above, calcium acetate 667 mg TID with meals, cholecalciferol 2000 units daily, acetaminophen 500 mg prn. Allergies: NKDA.

medications.reason: Replaced by calcium acetate per nephrology

medications.sig: Take 1 capsule by mouth three times daily with meals

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up after her nephrology visit on 7/31; letter came last week and reviewed with her.

GPA in remission per nephrology. Kidneys have settled at CKD stage 3b. Back at work half days. Still tired by mid-afternoon but a bit better week to week. Knee and wrist aches come and go, no swelling. Bowels a little slow; the cramping hasn't returned. No cough, no blood in sputum or urine. Weight down a few pounds since May.

Medication changes from nephrology entered: prednisone now 10 mg daily; calcium acetate 667 mg with each meal replaces the calcium carbonate; she is following the low-phosphate sheet. D3 2000 units continues. Rituximab next in November. Acetaminophen for the back, works well enough. No NSAIDs.

Exam: looks better than in May. No pallor today. Lungs clear. Heart regular. Joints without synovitis. No edema.

A/P
1. CKD 3b after ANCA GN: BMP today; nephrology following. Renal dosing for anything new; no NSAIDs.
2. GPA on prednisone and rituximab: per nephrology.
3. Low back pain: acetaminophen, stay under 3 g/day.
4. Mammogram due, ordered.
5. Vaccines: flu in October. Will plan pneumococcal and shingles vaccines at the next visit given the immunosuppression.
RTC in about 4 months.

documents.title: Nephrology lab results
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
Results from the 07/31/2025 nephrology draw, faxed for your records.
Phosphorus 5.0 mg/dL (high).
25-hydroxy vitamin D 38 ng/mL (sufficient).
1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D 14 pg/mL (low).
Nephrology comment: stores are adequate on D3; the low active form reflects reduced kidney activation in CKD. No calcitriol for now; continue current plan and recheck with her next visit.

documents.title: Vitamin D question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: The kidney office sent me my vitamin D results and one is low and one is fine. Does that mean I should take more D? I don't want to double up if it's not needed.

documents.title: RE: Vitamin D question
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good question. The one that is fine (25-hydroxy) is your stored vitamin D, and it shows the 2000 units you take is enough. The low one is the active form, which the kidneys make from the stored form. Because your kidneys are weaker, they make less of it, and more D3 wouldn't change that. Nephrology decided not to add anything for now. So: keep the same dose, nothing extra.

2. Immunosuppressed: PCV20 today. Shingrix #1 today, #2 in 2-6 months. Flu and COVID done in October.
3. Back: stable.
Follow up at her physical in the spring.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual exam. A year out from the GPA admission and doing well. Working full time. Energy about back to normal. No cough, no blood in sputum or urine, no sinus symptoms, no joint pain. Back: occasional ache, acetaminophen 1-2 tabs a few days a week, never near 3 g. Nephrology plan unchanged. Next rituximab 5/27.

Allergies: NKDA. Avoids NSAIDs.
Social: never smoker; wine maybe once a week.

PHQ-2 0.

1. Preventive: CMP, CBC with diff, lipids, A1c (on chronic prednisone). Mammogram due in September, ordered. Pap due 2027. Colonoscopy 2023 normal. Shingrix series and PCV20 complete. Flu and COVID in the fall.
2. GPA in remission, CKD 3b: per nephrology; creatinine with today's labs.

Follow-up visit in September.

documents.title: Nephrology clinic letter
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
Outside nephrology group. Visit 08/05/2026.

Dear colleague,
Ms. McGrath came in a little over a year after her 2025 hospitalization with PR3-ANCA vasculitis, pulmonary hemorrhage and crescentic GN. Her complaints this time are ongoing tiredness and being thirsty all the time. She is passing large amounts of urine and gets up several times each night to go. She is not deliberately pushing fluids; she just never feels satisfied.

Background: GPA in remission; CKD stage 3b; roughly 25 years of daily ibuprofen for back pain before 2025, none since.
Medications: prednisone 10 mg daily; rituximab 1000 mg IV every 6 months; calcium carbonate 600 mg TID with meals; cholecalciferol 2000 units daily; acetaminophen 500 mg as needed (max 3 g/day). NKDA.

Vitals within normal range. Examination unremarkable.
Serum sodium 150 mEq/L. Creatinine consistent with her known mild-to-moderate renal insufficiency.

Water deprivation test, then desmopressin, done under observation in our unit with hourly urine volumes and urine osmolality: urine osmolality reached only 210 mOsm/kg at the end of deprivation and 225 mOsm/kg after desmopressin, with urine output staying high.

Impression: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. The kidneys are not responding to ADH, which fits tubular injury from her prior disease.

Plan:
- Drink to thirst and keep water with her at all times; do not restrict fluids.
- Low-sodium diet, handout given.
- Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily started today.
- Repeat sodium with us in 2 weeks.
- Vasculitis plan unchanged.
Please continue to avoid NSAIDs.

documents.title: New diagnosis from kidney doctor
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Wanted you to know, the kidney doctor ran a test last week where I couldn't drink for hours and then got a shot. She says my kidneys can't hold onto water anymore, something called nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which is why I've been so thirsty and up all night. She started me on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg. Is that ok with everything else I take? Should I come in?

documents.title: RE: New diagnosis from kidney doctor
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks for the update, Dawn. Hydrochlorothiazide is the usual first medicine for this and it is fine alongside your other medicines. Keep water handy and drink whenever you're thirsty, and keep the sodium recheck with nephrology. We haven't received their note yet; I'll look for it. No need for an extra visit unless you feel dizzy, confused or can't keep up with your thirst; otherwise we'll go over it at your September appointment.
